title: The Association of Opening K-12 Schools with the Spread of COVID-19 in the United States: County-Level Panel Data Analysis
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether opening K-12 schools was associated with the spread of COVID-19 in U.S. counties during the 2020–2021 school reopening period. The authors ask whether school opening mode (in-person, hybrid, or remote) and mitigation measures such as staff mask requirements were related to subsequent changes in COVID-19 case and death growth rates.

The study uses county-level panel data from the United States, combining school opening and mitigation information from MCH Strategic Data with foot-traffic mobility data from SafeGraph and COVID-19 outcomes from the New York Times. The analysis covers April 1 to December 2, 2020 and compares counties over time using event-study models and debiased fixed-effects panel regressions. The main school-related exposures are K-12 visits and opening mode, with additional controls for NPIs, testing growth, county fixed effects, and state-week fixed effects.

The authors conclude that higher K-12 school visits and in-person openings are associated with increases in COVID-19 case growth, with stronger associations where staff mask mandates were absent. They also find that school openings are associated with higher workplace mobility, suggesting that reopening schools may have increased community transmission partly by enabling parents to return to work. Overall, the paper argues that school-based mitigation measures, especially masking, may reduce risk, but the findings remain observational and sensitive to unobserved confounding.
quality_tier_rationale: This paper is not about an AI or educational intervention; it is an observational epidemiological study of K-12 school openings and COVID-19 spread. While the methods are published and quantitative, they do not evaluate an education technology intervention relevant to the requested taxonomy.
impact_tier_rationale: There is no educational intervention effect to classify in this context. The paper’s findings concern public-health associations rather than K-12 learning outcomes or technology impact, so it has no applicable impact on the requested intervention domain.
limitations: observational and causal interpretation depends on unconfoundedness assumptions
possible endogeneity of school opening timing and teaching mode
